accuracy.evidence: Checked against NC Year 4 Living things and their habitats (food chains, producers, predators and prey; environments change), NGSS 5-LS2-1 and the BBC Bitesize KS2 food webs guide: arrows run from food to eater; producers photosynthesise; primary consumers eat producers; secondary consumers eat consumers; decomposers return nutrients to soil. The meadow web's roles were computed from its own arrows (grass, berries producers; rabbit, mouse, grasshopper primary; frog, snake, fox, hawk secondary) and its four hawk chains enumerated by hand. Removal effects follow the arrows only and are stated as likely changes, not certainties.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented food-web errors (Allen, 'Misconceptions in Primary Science'; Gallegos et al. on food-web reasoning): reading arrows as 'eats', calling an eaten plant a consumer, judging role by size, assuming a predator dies out when one prey goes (chain thinking), thinking only directly linked species are affected, and ignoring decomposers. Each is a prediction option, a tap message or a tagged challenge answer.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagfoodweb is a ten-node branching web where every action reads arrows in and out of a node: all eaters of one prey, roles computed from the web, a path builder that only accepts arrow-following taps to the hawk, two removals that highlight knock-on arrows, and a decomposer loop. flagchain works with single straight three-link chains and a gap to fill; it has no branching, no primary/secondary split and no chain tracing. Shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Taps are judged against the arrows, so learners discover direction (tapping berries for 'who eats the mouse' explains the arrow points into the mouse); the role step names why a big hawk and a small frog are both secondary consumers; two traced chains show the shared hawk; removing frogs lights the arrows to snake, hawk and grasshopper before the text sums up; the rabbit removal shows the fox switching to mice.

predictions.evidence: Six predictions with tempting wrong options: '1, the fox' eats the mouse, 'primary consumer' for the frog, 'just one' chain to the hawk, grasshoppers 'go down too', foxes 'all die straight away', and a dead hawk 'stays there for ever'. Each is disproved by its task.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions; wrong answers are tagged arrow, prod, big, same, link, chain or top, and each message names the slip: arrow direction, producers are plants, role from diet not size, prey rise when predators go, everything in a web is linked, predators switch food, decomposers versus top predators.

readability.evidence: Kid text Flesch-Kincaid grade 3.4 (family target ≤ 5), with one worked meadow example carried through; key idea 6.3; adult text 7.7 (≤ 10). Curriculum terms producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer and decomposer are each defined in a short sentence at first use.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passed: no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with any lesson, including 509 Simple Food Chains. Kid paragraphs: what a web is and arrow direction, roles, reading two chains, dependence and decomposers. Adult: placement, meaning, mistakes, what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots of all seven steps in both themes: the ten nodes and labels fit at 390 px with the canvas at 1.2 height ratio; the step heading and feedback line sit clear of the hawk and the producers; node buttons wrap three per row with emoji and names; highlighted arrows (green, blue, amber) stay distinct in dark mode.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas tap has a labelled button twin (one per living thing, plus Start again), the role step uses three labelled role buttons, and the dead-hawk drag has 'dead hawk → fungi/grass' and 'nutrients → …' buttons. The canvas aria-label repeats each feedback line. walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
